text: Real data is messy — extra whitespace, inconsistent casing, raw comma-separated lines. This lesson is about taming text: creating and indexing strings, cleaning them up with a handful of methods, pulling fields out of a raw line by hand, and building readable output with f-strings.

A string is text in single or double quotes — Python doesn't care which, as long as you're consistent. Plus joins strings together. And you can index into a string by position starting at zero, or grab a slice, like status zero to four, which runs up to but not including index four.

Four methods handle most messy text. Strip removes leading and trailing whitespace. Upper and lower normalize casing. Replace swaps characters, like turning spaces into underscores for a safe filename. Strip is especially important once you're reading real files in Chapter 3 — every line carries an invisible trailing newline that'll quietly break your comparisons.

Before you learn Python's built-in CSV reader in Chapter 3, it's worth seeing why it exists. A raw line from a file is just one long string, and split on a comma breaks it into a list of fields. Notice every field comes back as a string, even ones that look numeric — and this manual approach breaks the moment a field itself contains a comma.

An f-string lets you embed variables directly inside text with a simple f prefix — far more readable than building the same string with plus and str conversions. And f-strings support formatting right inside the braces: colon dot two f formats a float with exactly two decimal places, the standard way to display money so it never shows $129.9 or six zeros.

You can now clean, slice, split, and format text like a data engineer, not just a beginner. Next lesson: lists, tuples, and sets — three different ways to hold more than one value at a time, and when to reach for each one.
